conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states that current best evidence, particularly the updated 2023 Cochrane systematic review, supports a modest but real protective effect of cranberry products in preventing recurrent UTIs in women.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
I need to flag an important issue before presenting conclusions: the evidence I found does not support a "no" answer. In fact, the most authoritative source—the current Cochrane systematic review—concludes the opposite.

**What the evidence actually shows**

The updated 2023 Cochrane review (50 RCTs, 8,857 participants) found that cranberry products reduce UTI risk by roughly 26–30%, with a more pronounced benefit specifically in women with recurrent UTIs (risk ratio approximately 0.53 in this subgroup) ([cochrane.org](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001321_cranberries-preventing-urinary-tract-infections)). This is a meaningful revision from earlier Cochrane conclusions, which had found insufficient evidence of benefit ([thennt.com](https://thennt.com/nnt/cranberry-products-for-preventing-urinary-tract-infections/)); the newer, larger dataset shifted the evidence toward a modest but real protective effect in this population.

A biological rationale supports this: cranberry proanthocyanidins (PACs) inhibit P-fimbriated E. coli from adhering to bladder epithelial cells, the first step in UTI pathogenesis, giving plausibility to a preventive mechanism rather than merely correlation ([dovepress.com](https://www.dovepress.com/cranberry-products-in-the-prevention-of-urinary-tract-infections-exami-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-BTAT)).

However, benefit appears inconsistent across other groups—cranberry does not clearly help elderly people, pregnant women, or those with neuromuscular bladder dysfunction ([obgproject.com](https://www.obgproject.com/2023/05/10/cochrane-update-do-cranberry-products-reduce-the-risk-of-utis/)), and effect sizes vary by formulation (juice vs. tablets vs. concentrated PAC extracts) and dose.

**Conclusion**

Current best evidence indicates the answer is closer to "yes, modestly" for otherwise healthy women with recurrent UTIs—not "no." If you believed the answer was no, that reflects older or superseded evidence; the updated Cochrane meta-analysis reverses that prior consensus for this specific population, though effects are modest and product/dose-dependent.
